title: Learning from human preferences (RLHF, DPO)
summary: People judge better than they demonstrate, so preference tuning learns from comparisons. The Bradley-Terry model turns score differences into preference probabilities. RLHF trains a reward model on comparisons and then optimises the policy against it with a KL penalty to the reference model. DPO uses the closed-form optimum of that same objective to skip the reward model and train directly on the comparisons.
llm_link: Most chat models you use were tuned on preference comparisons after supervised fine-tuning. When a model's style shifts toward longer, more hedged or more agreeable answers, that is often the fingerprint of what the reward model (or the preference data behind DPO) rewarded.
key_ideas: Data: (prompt x, chosen y_w, rejected y_l).
Bradley-Terry: P(y_w ≻ y_l) = σ(r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l)). Only differences matter; adding a constant to every score changes nothing.
Reward model loss (InstructGPT): −log σ(r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l)).
RLHF objective: maximise E[r(x, y)] − β·KL(π ‖ π_ref). The KL term stops the policy from exploiting reward-model quirks and drifting from fluent text. InstructGPT optimised it with PPO.
InstructGPT: labellers preferred a 1.3B InstructGPT model over 175B GPT-3.
Closed-form optimum: π*(y|x) = π_ref(y|x)·exp(r(x, y)/β) / Z(x), so r(x, y) = β·log(π*(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)) + β·log Z(x).
DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023): substitute into Bradley-Terry; Z(x) cancels. Loss = −log σ(β[log π(y_w)/π_ref(y_w) − log π(y_l)/π_ref(y_l)]). No reward model, no sampling during training.

quiz.q: Predict the result: a reward model scores response A at 2.0 and response B at 2.0. Under Bradley-Terry, what is P(A preferred over B)?
quiz.explain: σ(2.0 − 2.0) = σ(0) = 0.5. Equal scores mean a coin flip; only the difference between scores matters.

quiz.q: If you add 10 to every score the reward model produces, what happens to the Bradley-Terry preference probabilities?
quiz.explain: Each probability depends on r_a − r_b, and the 10s cancel. This is also why the prompt-only term log Z(x) cancels in DPO.

quiz.q: Why does the RLHF objective subtract β·KL(π ‖ π_ref)?
options: To stop the policy from drifting far from the reference model, where it can exploit flaws in the reward model
Because PPO cannot work without it
quiz.explain: The reward model is only trustworthy near the kind of text it was trained on. The KL penalty keeps the policy close to the reference model so it cannot chase reward-model quirks.

quiz.q: In DPO, what replaces the separately trained reward model?
options: The implicit reward β·log(π(y|x)/π_ref(y|x)) computed from the policy and the frozen reference
quiz.explain: The closed-form optimum lets the reward be written through the policy's own log-probability ratio, so the comparison data can train the policy directly.

quiz.q: What did the InstructGPT paper report about model size and human preference?
options: Only models above 100B parameters benefit from RLHF
Labellers preferred outputs of a 1.3B InstructGPT model to those of 175B GPT-3
RLHF made models less preferred but more accurate
RLHF only works without supervised fine-tuning
quiz.explain: Alignment to what people prefer mattered more for their judgements than a hundredfold difference in parameters.

problems.title: Bradley-Terry and the reward-model loss
problems.prompt:
Write pref_prob(r_a, r_b), the probability that A is preferred: sigmoid(r_a − r_b) with sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)).

Then write rm_loss(r_chosen, r_rejected) = −log(pref_prob(r_chosen, r_rejected)), the reward model's loss on one comparison.

pref_prob(2.0, 2.0)   # 0.5
rm_loss(2.0, 2.0)     # 0.693... (log 2)

tests.name: equal scores are a coin flip
tests.code:
out = pref_prob(2.0, 2.0)
assert out is not None, 'pref_prob returned None'
assert abs(out - 0.5) < 1e-9, f'expected 0.5, got {out}'

tests.name: higher score wins more often
tests.code:
p = pref_prob(3.0, 1.0)
assert abs(p - 0.8807970779778823) < 1e-9, f'expected sigmoid(2) = 0.8808, got {p}. Did you compute r_a - r_b (not r_b - r_a)?'

tests.name: only differences matter
tests.code: assert abs(pref_prob(13.0, 11.0) - pref_prob(3.0, 1.0)) < 1e-12, 'adding 10 to both scores must not change the probability'

tests.name: loss at a tie is log 2
tests.code:
import math
out = rm_loss(2.0, 2.0)
assert out is not None, 'rm_loss returned None'
assert abs(out - math.log(2)) < 1e-9, f'expected log 2 = 0.693, got {out}'

tests.name: loss falls as the chosen score rises
tests.code: assert rm_loss(3.0, 0.0) < rm_loss(1.0, 0.0) < rm_loss(0.0, 1.0), 'the loss should shrink as the chosen response is ranked further above the rejected one'

hints: pref_prob is one line: return sigmoid(r_a - r_b)

problems.title: The DPO loss
problems.prompt:
For one comparison you are given four log-probabilities (each is the sum of the token log-probs of a whole response):

  • pc, pr: the policy's log-prob of the chosen and the rejected response
  • rc, rr: the frozen reference model's log-probs of the same two responses

Write implicit_reward(logp_policy, logp_ref, beta) = beta * (logp_policy − logp_ref), and dpo_loss(pc, pr, rc, rr, beta) = −log sigmoid(implicit_reward(pc, rc) − implicit_reward(pr, rr)).

dpo_loss(-10, -12, -10, -12, 0.1)   # 0.693...: the policy still equals the reference

tests.name: policy equal to reference gives log 2
tests.code:
import math
out = dpo_loss(-10, -12, -10, -12, 0.1)
assert out is not None, 'dpo_loss returned None'
assert abs(out - math.log(2)) < 1e-9, f'when the policy equals the reference both implicit rewards are 0, so the loss is log 2 = 0.693; got {out}'

tests.name: implicit reward
tests.code:
out = implicit_reward(-8.0, -10.0, 0.5)
assert out is not None and abs(out - 1.0) < 1e-9, f'expected 0.5 * (-8 - (-10)) = 1.0, got {out}'

tests.name: raising the chosen response lowers the loss
tests.code:
base = dpo_loss(-10, -12, -10, -12, 0.1)
better = dpo_loss(-8, -12, -10, -12, 0.1)
assert better < base, f'making the chosen response more likely than the reference does should lower the loss ({better} vs {base})'

tests.name: reference-only differences do not count
tests.code:
a = dpo_loss(-10, -12, -10, -12, 0.1)
b = dpo_loss(-10, -12, -11, -13, 0.1)
c = dpo_loss(-11, -13, -11, -13, 0.1)
assert abs(a - c) < 1e-12, 'shifting policy and reference by the same amount should not change the loss'
assert abs(b - dpo_loss(-9, -11, -10, -12, 0.1)) < 1e-12, 'only policy-minus-reference matters'

tests.name: value check
tests.code:
import math
out = dpo_loss(-9.0, -13.0, -10.0, -12.0, 0.5)
exp = -math.log(1 / (1 + math.exp(-(0.5 * 1 - 0.5 * -1))))
assert abs(out - exp) < 1e-9, f'expected {exp:.6f}, got {out}. The chosen implicit reward is 0.5, the rejected one is -0.5.'

hints: margin = implicit_reward(pc, rc, beta) - implicit_reward(pr, rr, beta)

problems.title: The KL-regularised optimum (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Pretend a prompt has only four possible responses. The reference model gives them probabilities ref and a reward model scores them r. The policy that maximises E[r] − β·KL(π ‖ π_ref) is

π*(y) = ref(y) · exp(r(y) / β) / Z, where Z makes the probabilities sum to 1.

Write optimal_policy(ref, r, beta) returning π* as a NumPy array. Then see the two extremes: a large β keeps π* near the reference, a small β piles everything on the best-scored response.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def optimal_policy(ref, r, beta):
    ref = np.asarray(ref, dtype=float)
    r = np.asarray(r, dtype=float)
    # TODO 1: unnormalised weights: ref * exp(r / beta)
    # TODO 2: divide by their sum (that sum is Z)
    pass

tests.name: sums to one
tests.code:
import numpy as np
p = optimal_policy([0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1], [1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 0.5], 1.0)
assert p is not None, 'optimal_policy returned None'
assert abs(np.sum(p) - 1) < 1e-9, f'probabilities must sum to 1, got {np.sum(p)}. Did you divide by Z?'

tests.name: known values
tests.code:
import numpy as np
ref = np.array([0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]); r = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 0.5])
w = ref * np.exp(r); exp = w / w.sum()
p = optimal_policy(ref, r, 1.0)
assert np.allclose(p, exp), f'expected {np.round(exp,4)}, got {np.round(p,4)}'

tests.name: large beta stays near the reference
tests.code:
import numpy as np
p = optimal_policy([0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1], [1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 0.5], 1000.0)
assert np.allclose(p, [0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1], atol=1e-2), f'with a strong leash (beta large) the policy should barely move from the reference, got {np.round(p,3)}'

tests.name: small beta picks the best response
tests.code:
import numpy as np
p = optimal_policy([0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1], [1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 0.5], 0.05)
assert p[2] > 0.99, f'with almost no leash the policy should put nearly all probability on response 2 (highest reward), got {np.round(p,3)}'

tests.name: reward is recoverable up to a constant
tests.code:
import numpy as np
ref = np.array([0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]); r = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 0.5]); b = 0.7
p = optimal_policy(ref, r, b)
implied = b * np.log(p / ref)
d = implied - r
assert np.allclose(d, d[0]), 'beta*log(pi*/ref) should equal the reward plus the same constant (-beta log Z) for every response; this is the identity DPO is built on'

hints: w = ref * np.exp(r / beta) works on whole arrays at once.
